analysis.one_liner: Requires large electricity and gas utilities to hit yearly customer energy-savings targets.
analysis.headline: The Senate Energy Committee held a single hearing on the bill in April 2009, never brought it to a vote, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a national energy efficiency standard for large retail electricity and natural gas distributors. Each utility would have to show, year by year, that its customers used cumulatively less energy than a set percentage of a baseline: reaching 15% electricity savings and 10% natural gas savings by 2020, with stricter targets set every decade after that. Utilities could count savings from better building codes, appliance standards, combined heat and power systems, and programs run by themselves, other utilities, states, or private efficiency companies, and could pay an alternative fee to states that fund efficiency programs instead. States could take over administering the program, and the Energy Department would enforce it with penalties and independent scientific reviews.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that use electricity and natural gas, since efficiency upgrades cost less than generating or delivering extra energy and the bill targeted only savings that were cheaper than supply. States would gain a funded role running efficiency programs and would receive alternative compliance payments to spend on them. A new market of energy service companies and third-party efficiency providers would be created, since utilities could buy verified savings from them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and businesses paying energy bills

how_it_helps.text: Sets rising cumulative savings targets for large utilities — 1% of baseline electricity savings in 2012 climbing to 15% by 2020, and 0.75% natural gas savings climbing to 10% — so energy demand shrinks steadily instead of growing [S3].

Limits the mandate to savings that are 'cost-effective' — meaning the lifetime benefits beat the lifetime costs — so customers are not forced to fund efficiency that costs more than the energy it saves [S3].

Lets states take over administration if their programs meet or exceed the federal standard, keeps state authority to set stricter rules intact, and routes alternative compliance payments into state efficiency programs [S3].

Creates a compliance market utilities can buy into: savings purchased from other distributors, states, or third-party efficiency providers count toward targets, with measurement, verification, and anti-double-counting rules to keep reported savings honest [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large retail electricity distributors (those delivering 1.5 million megawatt-hours or more over two years) and large natural gas distributors (over 5 billion cubic feet) would bear the cost of running efficiency programs, verifying savings, and paying penalties — up to $100 per megawatt-hour of missed electricity savings or $10 per million Btu of missed gas savings — if they fell short. Under traditional utility rate design, where revenue depends on units sold, mandating lower sales puts pressure on these companies' earnings, and some of those costs could be passed through to ratepayers.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls on utilities, and under conventional rate regulation utilities recover program costs through customer rates, so some of the cost would likely show up on bills even while total energy use — and total energy spending — falls [S3].

A uniform federal floor would overlay dozens of existing state efficiency programs; the bill directs regulators to preserve state program integrity, but utilities and state regulators would still face a second layer of federal reporting, review, and enforcement [S3].

The savings percentages are fixed in the bill through 2020 regardless of regional differences in climate, building stock, or how much cheap efficiency is left in a given state's system, which critics of one-size-fits-all standards point to as a fairness problem [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: efficiency is generally the cheapest energy resource available, and the bill restricted the mandate to savings cheaper than new supply, so most independent analyses of this type of standard find net savings for customers over time. The main honest objection is transition cost and complexity — utilities would spend on programs up front, recover it through rates, and every state would run the program under a federal overlay. On balance, a well-designed bill for billpayers, but the burden of proving savings falls on regulated companies and their regulators.

outcome.mechanism: After introduction the bill went to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which held one hearing in April 2009 and then never scheduled a vote on it, and the Congress ended with the bill still stuck there.

narrative.text: Senator Schumer introduced the bill on March 9, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S5].
The committee's only action was a hearing on April 22, 2009, printed as S.Hrg. 111-28; no markup, vote, or committee report followed [S5].
The bill attracted two cosponsors — one Senate Democrat and the chamber's lone Independent — and never reached the Senate floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large electricity and natural gas distributors came out ahead: no federal savings mandate, no penalties, and no requirement to shrink the volume of energy they sell. States and efficiency businesses also gained nothing, since the funded efficiency market the bill would have created never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large utilities kept their sales volumes untouched

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote ever occurred, so partisan lines were never tested; the bill's sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent, with no Republican support on record [S4].

industries.note: The bill obligated utilities delivering over 1.5 million megawatt-hours to cut cumulative customer consumption up to 15% by 2020 or pay penalties up to $100 per megawatt-hour short. Because utility revenue traditionally depends on kilowatt-hours sold, a mandate to sell less directly cuts into the volume that generates earnings.

Distributors delivering over 5 billion cubic feet faced a 10% cumulative savings requirement by 2020 and penalties of $10 per million Btu for shortfalls. Their business model, like electric utilities', is built on volumes delivered.

industries.industry: Energy service companies and third-party efficiency providers
industries.note: The bill explicitly let utilities meet targets by purchasing verified savings from third-party efficiency providers, creating a new compliance market for energy service companies, building owners, and financial institutions.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel power generators and gas producers
industries.note: A national standard that steadily shrinks electricity and natural gas demand reduces the need for new generation and fuel supply, trimming future sales for companies that produce and sell energy. Lower demand also means lower bills and less pollution for the public.
